title: Exploring the Application of Neurostructural Principles to the Design of Public Spaces on University Campuses
research_question: How can neurostructural principles be applied to the design of public spaces on university campuses to optimize students' learning efficiency, social interactions, and psychological well-being? Which design elements are effective in enhancing students' learning efficiency and emotional states, and what are students' main concerns about improvements to campus public spaces?

participants.description: Students enrolled at Hainan University in China. 50.64% female, 49.36% male. 86.38% were 18–24 years old. 25.71% were first-year university students.
participants.recruitment: Random sampling of students enrolled at Hainan University, distributed through China Questionnaire Star platform and on-campus channels.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Existing public learning spaces on Hainan University's Haidian Campus, China, specifically libraries, student centers, and open learning areas (including classrooms and study rooms).

Satisfaction with specific design elements (lighting, furniture, natural elements, materials/textures)

Multiple choice (silence, background music, natural sounds, don't care)

measures.construct: Preference for furniture configurations and layouts
measures.instrument: Multiple choice (single type, multiple types, modular, mobile furniture)
Multiple choice (linear/square, curved/irregular, symmetrical, asymmetrical, no preference)

measures.construct: Belief that design elements (furniture, sound, etc.) affect mood
Belief that building materials affect mood
Belief that light conditions with different color temperatures affect mental state
Perceived learning efficiency under natural vs. artificial light
measures.instrument: Multiple choice (natural light better, artificial light better, no difference)

measures.instrument: Multiple choice (positive impact, no impact, negative impact)

measures.construct: Perceived effectiveness of improvements for psychological stress reduction
measures.instrument: Multiple choice (increasing natural light, optimizing furniture, improving space layout, harmonious materials, adding natural elements)

measures.construct: Willingness to participate in design and feedback process for public learning spaces
Willingness to provide specific input for redesign
Willingness to use and evaluate neurostructural public learning spaces

mechanisms: Rational allocation of natural light, optimization of the acoustic environment, adoption of soothing color schemes, and flexible spatial layouts relieve students' psychological stress, enhance academic performance, and facilitate social interactions.
Natural light enhances students' emotional stability and reduces visual fatigue.
Flexible spatial layout and reasonable acoustic environment improve learning experience and social interaction.
Use of natural materials and natural elements enhances comfort and attractiveness of the learning space.

Design strategies based on neuro-architectural principles (optimizing campus spatial layout, enhancing natural lighting, improving spatial environment/configuration, adding natural elements) enhance students' learning efficiency, social interaction, and psychological well-being.
implementation_implications: Design strategies based on neuro-architectural principles can significantly enhance students' learning efficiency, social interaction, and psychological well-being in university campus spaces.
The findings provide a scientific basis and empirical support for designing university campus spaces based on user needs.
Future campus designs should fully consider the unique needs of university students regarding functionality, comfort, and social space concerns to promote sustainable development.
The study provides valuable references and insights for future campus planning and renovation, promoting the further application and development of neuroarchitecture in university campus design.

tables.description: Frequency analysis of space satisfaction for different learning spaces (Library, Interior, College specialized classrooms) across various satisfaction levels.
Survey data from the 'Interest' stage (Q9-Q13) showing student preferences for lighting, materials, sound, furniture configurations, and space shapes.
Results of user willingness to engage in different design elements for campus public space improvement.

limitations: The findings may not be fully applicable to other types of universities or different cultural environments due to the single case study (Hainan University).
The use of questionnaires and descriptive statistical methods (frequency analysis) may be affected by the subjectivity of participants and the representativeness of the sample.
Future studies could benefit from combining other research methods, such as observational and experimental methods, for more comprehensive and in-depth findings.

paper_metadata.title: Exploring the Application of Neurostructural Principles to the Design of Public Spaces on University Campuses
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Exploring the Application of Neurostructural Principles to the Design of Public Spaces on University Campuses
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In this study, we examined the application of neurostructural principles to the design of public spaces on university campuses to optimize students’ learning efficiency, social interactions, and psychological well-being. Using Hainan University in China as a case study, a descriptive analysis was used to evaluate the case study design of the data. Data on students’ preferences for and satisfaction with public learning spaces (libraries, student centers, and open learning areas) were also collected through a questionnaire. The questionnaire was based on the four stages of the AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, and Action) model and covered basic information about the participants and their first impressions of the learning spaces, design element preferences, emotional and cognitive influences, and willingness to participate in improving the design of campus spaces. Data were analyzed using quantitative methods, including frequency analysis and score aggregation, to assess the students’ satisfaction with the existing design elements of the learning space and their suggestions for potential improvements. A random sample of students enrolled at Hainan University was used to ensure that the data were representative. The results of the study indicate that the rational allocation of natural light, the optimization of the acoustic environment, the adoption of soothing color schemes, and flexible spatial layouts are effective at relieving students’ psychological stress, enhancing their academic performance, and facilitating social interactions. Some of the existing designs are already in line with neurostructural principles, but there is still room for improvement, especially in terms of color schemes and spatial configurations. Students have positive attitudes towards participating in campus space improvement, with especially high interest in light optimization, spatial layout, and the use of natural materials. This study verifies the effectiveness of using neural structure principles in campus public spaces by establishing an empirical model, proves its positive effect on the quality of the campus environment and students’ well-being, and provides empirical evidence and theoretical support for future campus design.
